extracted.intended_audience: general readers, political thinkers, abolitionists, and activists interested in civil disobedience
extracted.subtask_description: An argumentative/persuasive essay articulating the moral duty of individual conscience to resist and withdraw support from unjust government, with practical prescriptions (e.g., tax refusal, prison as protest).

rubrics_metrics.name: That government is best which governs least / not at all
rubrics_metrics.description: "That government is best which governs least;" ... carried out, it finally amounts to this ... "That government is best which governs not at all;" and when men are prepared for it, that will be the kind of government which they will have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government is an expedient and at best but temporary; aim for minimal or no government when people are prepared. Example/implication: prefer institutions that let people be largely left alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government is an expedient liable to abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The government itself ... is equally liable to be abused and perverted before the people can act through it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume government action is inherently virtuous; scrutinize its effects. The standing army is an arm of a standing government—institutions can be turned to unjust ends (example: the Mexican war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resign conscience to the legislator
rubrics_metrics.description: Must the citizen ever for a moment, or in the least degree, resign his conscience to the legislator? Why has every man a conscience, then? I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conscience should override legal obligation when law conflicts with justice. Anti-pattern: obeying law as a substitute for moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the right, not the law per se
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not desirable to cultivate a respect for the law, so much as for the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize moral rightness over legal obedience. Law may make men agents of injustice; thus legal compliance is not a moral measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: A man's only obligation is to do what he thinks right
rubrics_metrics.description: The only obligation which I have a right to assume, is to do at any time what I think right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual moral responsibility is primary; one must follow personal judgment of right even against social/legal pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule is not identical with justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A government in which the majority rule in all cases can not be based on justice ... majorities decide only those questions to which the rule of expediency is applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate democratic majorities with moral correctness. Conscience should guide decisions on rights beyond mere expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting and political participation are often insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: All voting is a sort of gaming ... It is only expressing to men feebly your desire that it should prevail. Even voting for the right is doing nothing for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral acts alone are weak moral acts; effective moral action requires personal, principled deeds rather than reliance on majority processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action from principle is essentially revolutionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Action from principle ... changes things and relations; it is essentially revolutionary ... It not only divided states and churches, it divides families; aye, it divides the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral action based on principle will have disruptive, transformative effects; expect division and sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of revolution exists when tyranny is unendurable
rubrics_metrics.description: All men recognize the right of revolution; that is, the right to refuse allegiance to and to resist the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government commits systemic injustice (examples: slavery, aggressive conquest), resistance and revolution are morally permissible and sometimes required.

rubrics_metrics.name: If law makes you the agent of injustice, break it
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is of such a nature that it requires you to be the agent of injustice to another, then, I say, break the law. Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral imperative justifies civil disobedience: refuse to participate in institutionalized injustice (practical prescription: deny compliance, refuse taxes that fund injustice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdraw support (personally and financially) from unjust government
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who call themselves abolitionists should at once effectually withdraw their support, both in person and property, from the government ... I meet this ... once a year, in the person of its tax-gatherer; ... the simplest, the most effectual ... mode ... is to deny it then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete tactic: refuse to pay taxes, resign offices, or withdraw material support as moral protest. Example: refusing poll-tax and being willing to face imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: One honest man constitutes a majority of one
rubrics_metrics.description: Moreover, any man more right than his neighbors constitutes a majority of one already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral action need not wait for consensus; the conviction and actions of a single principled individual are significant and foundational for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prison can be the proper place for a just person
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. The proper place today ... is in her prisons ... the only house in a slave-state in which a free man can abide with honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting imprisonment for conscience is a legitimate and powerful form of protest; being jailed can strengthen moral witness and public persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive conformity enables injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Law never made men a whit more just; and, by means of their respect for it, even the well-disposed are daily made the agents of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive compliance or unreflective respect for institutions is morally dangerous; vigilance and refusal of complicity are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: The State enforces by physical force, not moral superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the state never intentionally confronts a man's sense, intellectual or moral, but only his body, his senses. It is not armed with superior wit or honesty, but with superior physical strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of state power and its reliance on coercion; moral resistance targets legitimacy rather than physical force (but must acknowledge possible physical reprisals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reforms require the few to act, not many to merely opine
rubrics_metrics.description: There are thousands who are in opinion opposed to slavery and to the war, who yet in effect do nothing ... They hesitate, and they regret, and sometimes they petition; but they do nothing in earnest and with effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of performative or purely opinionated opposition: effective change requires courageous deeds from a minority, not mere sympathetic opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral remedy should not be deferred by expediency calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Paley ... resolves all civil obligation into expediency ... But Paley appears never to have contemplated those cases to which the rule of expediency does not apply, in which a people, as well as an individual, must do justice, cost what it may.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce justice to cost–benefit calculations; some moral duties must be performed regardless of expense or danger.
